title: Dams in distress: Adult sex ratio, female nutritional condition, and population dynamics in mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus)
content:
Across mule deer populations in Utah, higher male:female ratios were associated with lower summer gain in body fat in adult females and with lower female population growth the following year. These associations suggest that management that increases the proportion of males may involve a demographic trade-off.


Abstract

Males and females of sexually dimorphic ungulates exhibit distinct competitive abilities due to differences in body size, digestive function and role in reproduction. In the attempt to enhance the hunting experience or manipulate population dynamics, management may favour increasing the proportion of either sex. Depending on the relationship between the sexes, management practices may have different consequences for individuals and populations. Females are often considered the primary drivers of population dynamics of polygynous ungulates. The role of males is often overlooked, but mounting evidence suggests that the proportion of males within a population may have important effects on population dynamics, either because of impacts on mating systems or intersexual competition. The effect of males within ungulate populations may thus have important implications for management, particularly when intersexual interactions influence females. We used long-term data on productivity (2007–2022) and body reserve dynamics (2015–2022) to quantify the influence of an increase in male proportion on population dynamics of free-ranging mule deer Odocoileus hemionus. We examined if an increasing male proportion, in relation to population density, influenced: (i) individual females through a change in body reserve accumulation; (ii) female population growth rate. Higher male:female ratios were associated with reduced seasonal body fat accumulation in females. Similarly, higher male:female ratios were associated with lower female population growth rates in the following year, consistent with a potential carry-over effect mediated through female body condition. Changes in male proportion affected body fat reserve accumulation and female population growth rate after accounting for climatic variation and density, at least with the levels observed in the study populations. Practical implication: A common shift in management of mule deer over the late 20th century has been an increase in the proportion of mature males in the population (i.e., higher male:female ratio). Our results suggest that such a management strategy may involve demographic trade-offs, being associated with reduced female body condition and lower population productivity. These findings are increasingly pertinent as mule deer populations appear to be declining in many areas.
